_comment: Eastern Cape Department of Education Grade 11 Geography P2 (Development Geography, Resources and Sustainability and Geographical Skills and Techniques), November 2025 provincial common examination.
Questions and marking-guideline answers extracted from the text layer of the official PDFs
(paper2.pdf, paper2_memo.pdf) and read against the rendered pages. Figures, maps,
graphs and photographs are described in [FIGURE: ...] brackets inside 'context'. memo_answer is
from the official marking guideline (English); mark allocations such as (2) are kept, one
accepted point per line. Column A/B items use the Grade 12 '[Y ... / Z ...]' style.
FORMAT: Section A Question 1 Development Geography (60) and Question 2 Resources and
Sustainability (60); Section B Question 3 Geographical Skills and Techniques (30) on the 1:50 000
topographical map 2529CC EMALAHLENI and the 1:10 000 orthophoto map 2529CC 15 EMALAHLENI. All three
questions are compulsory (150). The map sheet ships as a separate PDF inside the question-paper zip
(paper_download_url); it is not tracked here because of its size (about 51 MB), so map-read inputs
come from the memo's accepted values.

questions.context: 1.3 Refer to the extract below on community-based development and answer the questions that follow. FAILURE OF COMMUNITY-OWNED MACADAMIA NUT FARM: The Ncera Macadamia Nut Farm was launched in 2006 as a model of community-based rural development, aiming to empower local people. To support the project's development, it initially received over R135 million in investment. The money was sourced primarily from government departments and other public sector and development partners. In line with the principles of community-driven development, ownership of the farm was transferred to the Ncera community under the leadership of the Imidushane Council. Despite its ambitious goals, the nut farm struggled to gain momentum (success). It eventually collapsed in 2024 due to a combination of factors, including mismanagement of funds, government delays in infrastructure, limited skills among workers and a crash in macadamia nut prices. [Adapted from www.bizcommunity.com]

questions.context: 1.4 Refer to the image and extract on South African trading relationships. [FIGURE: a smartphone and laptop showing the TEMU and SHEIN apps with 'ONLINE SHOPPING' and 'BUY NOW' buttons, surrounded by parcels stamped 'MADE IN CHINA'.] BALANCING CONSUMER GAINS AND LOCAL INDUSTRY COSTS: Major online retailers* Shein and Temu have rapidly expanded their presence in South Africa. Since entering the market in 2020 and 2023 respectively, they have captured over a third of online clothing sales, and in 2024, generated an estimated R7,3 billion. Their success was driven by South Africa's previous customs relief system, which let imports under R500 be charged only a 20% import duty (tariff) without VAT. This kept prices low and allowed them to sell goods much cheaper than local competitors. It has now been proposed to the South African government that customs relief be removed so that every imported item will be charged both the 20% import duty (tariff) and the 15% VAT. * Online retailer: business that sells goods to consumers over the internet. questions.context: 2.3 Refer to the map and extract below based on soil erosion in South Africa. [FIGURE: map SOIL EROSION (IN HECTARES) PER PROVINCE with eroded areas shaded: Northern Cape 160 885; Eastern Cape 151 759; KwaZulu-Natal 87 522; Free State 64 674; Limpopo 58 669; Western Cape 25 403; Mpumalanga 17 420; North West 10 782; Gauteng 110.] Although soil erosion is a natural process worsened by climate change, human activities such as overgrazing, deforestation and poor farming practices accelerate erosion. Agricultural intensification often removes natural vegetation, exposing soil to erosion. As soil forms very slowly, it is considered a non-renewable resource and its loss reduces productivity and threatens food security. South Africa's average soil loss rate is 12,6 tons per hectare annually, while the natural formation rate is approximately 4,9 tons per hectare per year. This imbalance highlights the urgent need for better land management efforts. [Adapted from https://www.grainsa.co.za/soil-erosion-in-south-africa]

questions.context: 2.5 Refer to the extract on energy management in South Africa. SOUTH AFRICA’S CLIMATE CHANGE ACT: A GREENER FUTURE Adopted on 18 July 2024, South Africa’s Climate Change Act marks a major turning point in the country’s move towards a greener economy. The Act sets an ambitious target: achieving net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2050. It introduces a multi-tiered governance model that clearly defines responsibilities across different levels of government. Additionally, the Act sets sector-specific GHG reduction targets, encouraging businesses to adopt cleaner practices. This shift is expected to attract both local and international investment ─ particularly in renewable energy sectors such as solar and wind ─ while also strengthening energy security and reducing dependence on coal. At the individual level, the Act promotes energy-conscious living. [Adapted from www.south-africas-climate-change-act-paradigm-shift-energy]

questions.context: SECTION B. QUESTION 3: GEOGRAPHICAL SKILLS AND TECHNIQUES. GENERAL INFORMATION ON EMALAHLENI: [FIGURE: outline map of South Africa's provinces with Emalahleni marked by a dot in Mpumalanga.] Coordinates: 25°52'22"S; 29°15'19"E. Emalahleni, formerly known as Witbank, is a city in Mpumalanga whose name is derived from the Nguni language, means 'place of coal'. It is one of South Africa's major coal-mining hubs. The city is home to several large Eskom coal-fired power stations that contribute significantly to the country's electricity supply. Emalahleni also benefits from a well-developed transport infrastructure, with railway lines connecting it to Pretoria and the Maputo Port in Mozambique. Additionally, the convergence of the N4 and N12 highways supports the efficient transport of coal and other goods. The following English terms and their Afrikaans translations are shown on the topographical map: Conveyor Belt - Vervoerband; Diggings - Uitgrawings; Opencast Mine - Oopgroefmyn; Slimes Dams - Slykdamme; Stadium - Stadion. | 3.1 MAPWORK SKILLS AND CALCULATIONS.
